Homarus gammarus , known as the European lobster or common lobster , is a species of clawed lobster from the eastern Atlantic Ocean , Mediterranean Sea and parts of the Black Sea . It is closely related to the American lobster , H. americanus . It may grow to a length of 60 cm ( 24 in ) and a mass of 6 kilograms ( 13 lb ) , and bears a conspicuous pair of claws . In life , the lobsters are blue , only becoming " lobster red " on cooking . Mating occurs in the summer , producing eggs which are carried by the females for up to a year before hatching into planktonic larvae . Homarus gammarus is a highly esteemed food , and is widely caught using lobster pots , mostly around the British Isles . 
 Homarus gammarus is a large crustacean , with a body length up to 60 centimetres ( 24 in ) and weighing up to 5 – 6 kilograms ( 11 – 13 lb ) , although the lobsters caught in lobster pots are usually 23 – 38 cm ( 9 – 15 in ) long and weigh 0 @.@ 7 – 2 @.@ 2 kg ( 1 @.@ 5 – 4 @.@ 9 lb ) . Like other crustaceans , lobsters have a hard exoskeleton which they must shed in order to grow , in a process called ecdysis ( moulting ) . This may occur several times a year for young lobsters , but decreases to once every 1 – 2 years for larger animals . 
 The first pair of pereiopods is armed with a large , asymmetrical pair of claws . The larger one is the " crusher " , and has rounded nodules used for crushing prey ; the other is the " cutter " , which has sharp inner edges , and is used for holding or tearing the prey . Usually , the left claw is the crusher , and the right is the cutter . 
 The exoskeleton is generally blue above , with spots that coalesce , and yellow below . The red colour associated with lobsters only appears after cooking . This occurs because , in life , the red pigment astaxanthin is bound to a protein complex , but the complex is broken up by the heat of cooking , releasing the red pigment . 
 The closest relative of H. gammarus is the American lobster , Homarus americanus . The two species are very similar , and can be crossed artificially , although hybrids are unlikely to occur in the wild since their ranges do not overlap .  Female H. gammarus reach sexual maturity when they have grown to a carapace length of 80 – 85 millimetres ( 3 @.@ 1 – 3 @.@ 3 in ) , whereas males mature at a slightly smaller size . Mating typically occurs in summer between a recently moulted female , whose shell is therefore soft , and a hard @-@ shelled male . The female carries the eggs for up to 12 months , depending on the temperature , attached to her pleopods . Females carrying eggs are said to be " berried " and can be found throughout the year . 
 The eggs hatch at night , and the larvae swim to the water surface where they drift with the ocean currents , preying on zooplankton . This stage involves three moults and lasts for 15 – 35 days . After the third moult , the juvenile takes on a form closer to the adult , and adopts a benthic lifestyle . The juveniles are rarely seen in the wild , and are poorly known , although they are known to be capable of digging extensive burrows . It is estimated that only 1 larva in every 20 @,@ 000 survives to the benthic phase . When they reach a carapace length of 15 mm ( 0 @.@ 59 in ) , the juveniles leave their burrows and start their adult lives .

It is also present in most of the Mediterranean Sea , only missing from the section east of Crete , and along only the north @-@ west coast of the Black Sea .  The species can be divided into four genetically distinct populations , one widespread population , and three which have diverged due to small effective population sizes , possibly due to adaptation to the local environment . The first of these is the population of lobsters from northern Norway , which have been referred to as the " midnight @-@ sun lobster " . The populations in the Mediterranean Sea are distinct from those in the Atlantic Ocean . The last distinct population is found in the Netherlands : samples from the <unk> were distinct from those collected in the North Sea or English Channel . 
 Attempts have been made to introduce H. gammarus to New Zealand , alongside other European species such as the edible crab , Cancer pagurus . Between 1904 and 1914 , one million lobster larvae were released from hatcheries in Dunedin , but the species did not become established there . 
 Adult H. gammarus live on the continental shelf at depths of 0 – 150 metres ( 0 – 492 ft ) , although not normally deeper than 50 m ( 160 ft ) . They prefer hard substrates , such as rocks or hard mud , and live in holes or crevices , emerging at night to feed .

 Air Vice Marshal Frank Headlam , CB , CBE ( 15 July 1914 – 23 December 1976 ) was a senior commander in the Royal Australian Air Force ( RAAF ) . Born and educated in Tasmania , he joined the RAAF as an air cadet in January 1934 . He specialised in flying instruction and navigation before the outbreak of World War II . In April 1941 , he became commanding officer of No. 2 Squadron , which operated Lockheed Hudsons . The squadron was deployed to Dutch Timor in December , and saw action against Japanese forces in the South West Pacific . After returning to Australia in February 1942 , Headlam held staff appointments and training commands , finishing the war a group captain . 
 Headlam served as Officer Commanding North @-@ Western Area in 1946 , and as Director of Training from 1947 to 1950 . In 1950 – 51 , during the Malayan Emergency , he was stationed at Singapore as commander of No. 90 ( Composite ) Wing and , later , RAF Tengah . He twice served as acting Air Member for Personnel , in 1957 and 1959 – 60 , receiving appointment as a Commander of the Order of the British Empire in 1958 . Promoted air vice marshal , he successively held the positions of Air Officer Commanding ( AOC ) Operational Command in 1961 – 62 , AOC No. 224 Group RAF from 1962 to 1965 during the Indonesia – Malaysia Konfrontasi , Deputy Chief of the Air Staff in 1965 – 66 , and AOC Support Command in 1966 – 67 . He was appointed a Companion of the Order of the Bath in 1965 . Following a posting to London as Head of the Australian Joint Services Staff from 1968 to 1971 , he retired from the Air Force and died in Melbourne five years later . 
 The son of farmers Malcolm and Hilda Headlam , Frank Headlam was born on 15 July 1914 in Launceston , Tasmania . He was schooled at <unk> College , Hobart , and matriculated in 1932 . He underwent flying instruction with No. 1 Flying Training School ( FTS ) at RAAF Point Cook , Victoria , and was commissioned as a pilot officer on 1 January 1935 .

No larger than a flight according to the official history of the pre @-@ war RAAF , Seaplane Squadron was part of No. 1 FTS and operated Supermarine Southampton flying boats and de Havilland Gipsy Moth floatplanes , among other types . During this posting Headlam was promoted to flying officer , on 1 July 1935 , and wrote a paper on national defence in which he suggested that with " strong air forces , naval forces ( including submarines ) , and fixed defences , Australia may be made practically invulnerable " . According to Air Force historian Alan Stephens , this paper " in effect , defined the ' anti @-@ lodgment ' concept which has been a persistent feature of RAAF strategic thinking " . 
 Headlam completed a flying instructors course in July 1936 and joined the staff of No. 1 FTS . He was promoted to flight lieutenant on 1 March 1937 . Commencing in July 1938 , he was one of six students to take part in the RAAF 's first Long Specialist Navigation Course , run by Flight Lieutenants Bill Garing and Alister Murdoch at Point Cook . The course involved several epic training flights that attracted considerable media attention , including a twelve @-@ day , 10 @,@ 800 @-@ kilometre ( 6 @,@ 700 mi ) round @-@ Australia trip by three Avro Ansons , one of which was piloted by Headlam , in November . The following month , Headlam led the three Ansons on a six @-@ day journey back and forth over Central Australia . He subsequently passed the navigation course with a special distinction . On 27 January 1939 he was posted to RAAF Station Laverton , Victoria , as a flight commander . He served initially with No. 2 Squadron , before transferring to No. 1 Squadron on 29 August . Both units operated Ansons . 
 Following the outbreak of World War II , No. 1 Squadron was engaged in convoy escort and maritime reconnaissance duties off south @-@ eastern Australia . Headlam continued to serve with the squadron as a flight commander until 15 January 1940 , when he was assigned to Headquarters Laverton as the station navigation officer . On 27 March he was posted to the staff of RAAF Headquarters , Melbourne . He was promoted to squadron leader on 1 June 1940 . Two weeks later he married Katherine Bridge at St Paul 's Anglican Church in Frankston ; the couple would have a son and a daughter . 
 Headlam was given command of No. 2 Squadron at Laverton on 15 April 1941 , and raised to wing commander on 1 July . Equipped with Lockheed Hudsons , the squadron mainly conducted maritime patrols in southern waters until 5 December , when four of its aircraft were ordered to Darwin , Northern Territory , in response to fears of Japanese aggression in the Pacific . On 7 December , this detachment established itself at Penfui , near Koepang in Dutch Timor , while No. 2 Squadron 's eight remaining Hudsons were stationed at Darwin on standby . The following day , aware that Australia was now at war in the Pacific , one of the Penfui @-@ based Hudsons attacked the Japanese <unk> Nanyo Maru , which was suspected of being a radio ship , and forced it aground . By 12 December , Headlam had transferred to Penfui as commanding officer of the base , as well as No. 2 Squadron .

Eastern Area Command , considered a de facto operational headquarters owing to the preponderance of combat units under its control , was reorganised as Home Command in October 1953 . He was promoted to acting air commodore in May . His appointment as aide @-@ de @-@ camp to Queen Elizabeth II was announced on 7 October 1954 . 
 Headlam was promoted to substantive air commodore on 1 January 1955 . In November he was posted to RAAF Overseas Headquarters , London , and the following year undertook studies at the Imperial Defence College . Returning to Australia , he served as acting Air Member for Personnel at the Department of Air , Canberra , from 19 March to 21 October 1957 , between the terms of Air Vice Marshals Fred Scherger and Allan Walters , and again from 24 August 1959 to 28 March 1960 , between the terms of Walters and Air Vice Marshal Bill Hely . In this role Headlam occupied a seat on the Air Board , the service 's controlling body that comprised its senior officers and was chaired by the Chief of the Air Staff . He was also one of two RAAF representatives to serve on a committee , chaired by businessman William John Allison , examining conditions of defence service ; the committee 's recommendations led to a doubling of flight pay , among other improvements . Headlam 's other positions at the Department of Air included Air Commodore Plans from October 1957 to January 1959 , and Director General Plans and Policy from January to August 1959 . The latter assignment put him in charge of the RAAF 's Directorate of Intelligence . Headlam was appointed a Commander of the Order of the British Empire ( CBE ) in the 1958 Queen 's Birthday Honours , gazetted on 3 June . In May 1960 he became acting Deputy Chief of the Air Staff . 
 On 30 January 1961 , Headlam joined the staff of Operational Command ( OPCOM ) , the successor organisation to Home Command , responsible for the direction of RAAF operational units . He took over as Air Officer Commanding ( AOC ) OPCOM from Air Vice Marshal Val Hancock in April . Headlam was promoted to air vice marshal on 29 May . On 17 July 1962 , he was posted to RAAF Base Butterworth , Malaya , and took up the appointment of AOC No. 224 Group RAF in Singapore one week later . He was succeeded as AOC OPCOM by Air Vice Marshal Alister Murdoch . As AOC No. 224 Group , Headlam had overall responsibility for regional air defence and offensive air operations during the Brunei Rebellion in December 1962 , and the subsequent Konfrontasi between Indonesia and Malaysia that officially began the following month . Divorced from his first wife in 1956 , he married widowed social worker Vernon Spence at the Sydney registry office on 20 January 1964 . He handed over No. 224 Group to Air Vice Marshal Christopher Foxley @-@ Norris on 30 November . 
 Returning to Australia , Headlam became Deputy Chief of the Air Staff ( DCAS ) on 26 January 1965 . He was appointed a Companion of the Order of the Bath ( CB ) " in recognition of distinguished service in the Borneo Territories " on 22 June . His tenure as DCAS coincided with the most significant rearmament program the Air Force had undertaken since World War II , and with manpower shortages stemming from this expansion and from Australia 's increasing involvement in the security of South East Asia . The first RAAF helicopters were committed to the Vietnam War towards the end of his term , and he travelled to Saigon with the Chief of the General Staff , Lieutenant General Sir John Wilton , in March 1966 to plan the deployment . The year before , Wilton had recommended to Air Marshal Murdoch , the Chief of the Air Staff , that two Iroquois be sent to Vietnam for familiarisation purposes ; Murdoch had rebuffed Wilton , and the RAAF helicopter squadron was considered underprepared for its army co @-@ operation role when it finally did deploy . On 1 January 1968 , Headlam was posted to London as Head of the Australian Joint Services Staff . He served as an Extra Gentleman Usher to the Queen from 17 November 1970 to 5 June 1971 . 
 Returning to Australia in June 1971 , Headlam took resettlement leave before retiring from the Air Force on 3 August . He made his home in Melbourne , where he died aged 62 on 23 December 1976 , after a lengthy battle with cancer . Survived by his children and his second wife , he was given a private funeral and cremated at Springvale Crematorium .

 The current M @-@ 82 dates back to 1926 . It ran from US 31 in Hart to the northern junction of US 131 and M @-@ 46 in Howard City . Air Vice Marshal Frank Headlam, CB, CBE (15 July 1914 – 23 December 1976) held a senior position in the Royal Australian Air Force (RAAF). He was raised in Tasmania and joined the RAAF as an air cadet in January 1934. Before the onset of World War II, he dedicated himself to flight training and navigation skills. In April 1941, he assumed command of No. 2 Squadron, which flew Lockheed Hudson aircraft. The squadron was deployed to Dutch Timor in December, where it saw action against Japanese forces in the South West Pacific. Following his return to Australia in February 1942, Headlam took on several staff and training roles, eventually finishing the war with the rank of group captain.

In 1946, Headlam served as the Officer Commanding for the North Western Area, and from 1947 until 1950, he took on the role of Director of Training. During the Malayan Emergency from 1950 to 1951, he was based in Singapore, where he led No. 90 (Composite) Wing and subsequently RAF Tengah. He served as Air Member for Personnel on two separate occasions, first in 1957 and again from 1959 to 1960. He was named Commander of the Order of the British Empire in 1958. After his promotion to air vice marshal, he held various significant positions, including Air Officer Commanding (AOC) Operational Command from 1961 to 1962, AOC No. 224 Group RAF from 1962 to 1965 during the Indonesia-Malaysia Konfrontasi, Deputy Chief of the Air Staff from 1965 to 1966, and AOC Support Command from 1966 to 1967. In 1965, he was also appointed a Companion of the Order of the Bath. After leading the Australian Joint Services Staff in London from 1968 to 1971, he retired from the Air Force and passed away in Melbourne five years later.

Frank Headlam was born on July 15, 1914, in Launceston, Tasmania, to farmers Malcolm and Hilda Headlam. He graduated from <unk> College in Hobart in 1932. Against his parents' wishes, he joined the Royal Australian Air Force (RAAF) as an air cadet on January 16, 1934. Frank underwent his flight training at No. 1 Flying Training School (FTS) at RAAF Point Cook in Victoria and was appointed as a pilot officer on January 1, 1935.

Upon finishing a conversion course, Headlam was assigned to the Seaplane Squadron at Point Cook. The official history of the Royal Australian Air Force (RAAF) prior to World War II notes that the Seaplane Squadron had a limited number of aircraft and was integrated into No. 1 Flying Training School, operating planes such as the Supermarine Southampton flying boats and de Havilland Gipsy Moth floatplanes, among others. During this period, Headlam was promoted to flying officer on July 1, 1935, and wrote a paper on national defense in which he contended that Australia could be rendered nearly invulnerable through "robust air forces, naval forces (including submarines), and fixed defenses." Air Force historian Alan Stephens noted that this paper "effectively defined the 'anti-lodgment' concept, which has been a consistent element of RAAF strategic thought."

In July 1936, Headlam finished a flying instructor course and then became a member of No. 1 FTS. He was elevated to flight lieutenant on March 1, 1937. Starting in July 1938, he took part in the RAAF's first Long Specialist Navigation Course, led by Flight Lieutenants Bill Garing and Alister Murdoch at Point Cook. This course included several notable training flights that attracted significant media coverage, such as a remarkable twelve-day, 10,800-kilometre (6,700 mi) trip around Australia in November, during which Headlam flew one of three Avro Ansons. The following month, he led the three Ansons on a six-day mission over Central Australia. He performed exceptionally well in the navigation course, earning special recognition for his achievements. On January 27, 1939, he was posted to RAAF Station Laverton in Victoria as a flight commander. He initially worked with No. 2 Squadron before transferring to No. 1 Squadron on August 29, with both squadrons operating Ansons.

Following the outbreak of World War II, No. 1 Squadron participated in convoy escort and maritime reconnaissance missions along the southeastern coast of Australia. Headlam remained a flight commander within the squadron until January 15, 1940, when he was reassigned to Headquarters Laverton to take on the role of station navigation officer. On March 27, he joined the staff at RAAF Headquarters in Melbourne. He was elevated to the rank of squadron leader on June 1, 1940. Just two weeks afterward, he married Katherine Bridge at St Paul's Anglican Church in Frankston, and they would eventually have a son and a daughter.

On 15 April 1941, Headlam assumed command of No. 2 Squadron stationed at Laverton and was elevated to wing commander on 1 July. The squadron, equipped with Lockheed Hudsons, mainly conducted maritime patrols in southern waters until 5 December, when four of its aircraft were sent to Darwin, Northern Territory, amid fears of possible Japanese aggression in the Pacific. On 7 December, this contingent commenced operations at Penfui, close to Koepang in Dutch Timor, while the remaining eight Hudsons of No. 2 Squadron stayed on standby in Darwin. The following day, after confirming that Australia was officially engaged in war in the Pacific, one of the Hudsons at Penfui targeted the Japanese ship Nanyo Maru, suspected of being a radio vessel, and successfully drove it aground. By 12 December, Headlam had relocated to Penfui, taking on the role of commanding officer for both the base and No. 2 Squadron.

In January 1942, No. 2 Squadron's aircraft were located at Penfui, <unk> Island, and Darwin. The unit at Penfui was involved in operations targeting Japanese shipping related to the invasion of the Celebes. On January 11, two Hudson bombers engaged three Japanese floatplanes that were attacking a transport ship, successfully shooting down or damaging some of the enemy aircraft. However, the next day, both Hudsons were shot down by Mitsubishi Zeros. The Japanese carried out their first bombing raid on Penfui on January 26, 1942, and subsequent attacks resulted in damage to several aircraft. The operational Hudsons were then relocated to Darwin, while Headlam and his crew remained at Penfui to conduct reconnaissance flights from Australia. On February 18, Headlam received orders to evacuate all personnel except for a small team to assist Sparrow Force in demolishing the airfield. He returned to Darwin the following day, coinciding with the city’s first Japanese air raid. During this attack, four Hudsons from No. 2 Squadron were destroyed, prompting the remaining planes to be moved to Daly Waters, where they continued reconnaissance and bombing missions against Japanese forces in Timor.

Headlam served as the Controller of Operations at Headquarters North-Western Area Command in Darwin until May 12, 1942, when he was transferred to Nhill, Victoria, to take on the role of commanding officer of No. 2 Air Navigation School, which operated Ansons. In June, the personnel from this school formed No. 97 (Reserve) Squadron. On July 20, 1943, Headlam took command of No. 2 Air Observer School ( <unk> ), also utilizing Ansons and located in Mount Gambier, South Australia. He was promoted to group captain on December 1, 1943, and on December 9, he became the inaugural commanding officer of No. 3 <unk>, which operated Ansons and Fairey Battles from Port Pirie. After transferring command of No. 3 <unk>, he commenced his studies at RAAF Staff School in Mount Martha, Victoria, on October 2, 1944. On January 12, 1945, he was appointed as the senior administrative staff officer at North-Western Area Command.

In January 1946, Headlam was appointed as the Officer Commanding of the North Western Area. By the end of that year, he was reassigned to Britain, where he attended the Royal Air Force Staff College in Andover and collaborated with the RAAF Overseas Headquarters in London. After returning to Australia in November 1947, he became the Director of Training at RAAF Headquarters. In November 1950, he replaced Group Captain Paddy Heffernan as the head of No. 90 (Composite) Wing, stationed at RAF Changi in Singapore. No. 90 Wing was responsible for RAAF units involved in the Malayan Emergency, including No. 1 (Bomber) Squadron, which utilized Avro Lincolns, and No. 38 (Transport) Squadron, which operated Douglas C-47 Dakotas. The Lincolns conducted area bombing in areas controlled by communists and targeted specific sites, while the Dakotas were tasked with courier missions, transporting VIPs, executing medical evacuations across Southeast Asia, airlifting troops and supplies, and distributing propaganda leaflets in Malaya. On December 20, Headlam incurred minor injuries when a Dakota from No. 38 Squadron, which he was co-piloting during a supply drop, crash-landed in Kampong Aur, Pahang, due to an engine failure. In August 1951, he was appointed as the commander of RAF Tengah in Singapore while still overseeing No. 90 Wing, which he formally relinquished in December 1951.

On February 19, 1952, Headlam assumed the position of senior air staff officer (SASO) at Eastern Area Command in Penrith, New South Wales. During his tenure as SASO, the Royal Australian Air Force (RAAF) began upgrading its fleet with English Electric Canberra jet bombers and CAC Sabre jet fighters. The Air Force also underwent a major organizational transformation, transitioning from a geography-based command-and-control system to a functionally organized framework. This change resulted in the establishment of Home (operational), Training, and Maintenance Commands. In October 1953, Eastern Area Command, which had been effectively functioning as an operational headquarters due to its oversight of numerous combat units, was reorganized into Home Command. In acknowledgment of his "exceptional ability and devotion to duty," Headlam was honored as an Officer of the Order of the British Empire (OBE) in the 1954 New Year Honours. He was elevated to acting air commodore in May, and on October 7, 1954, it was revealed that he would serve as aide-de-camp to Queen Elizabeth II.

On January 1, 1955, Headlam was promoted to the position of substantive air commodore. Later that November, he was assigned to the RAAF Overseas Headquarters in London, and the subsequent year, he began his studies at the Imperial Defence College. Upon returning to Australia, he assumed the role of Air Member for Personnel at the Department of Air in Canberra from March 19 to October 21, 1957, serving in an interim capacity between Air Vice Marshals Fred Scherger and Allan Walters, and again from August 24, 1959, to March 28, 1960, between Walters and Air Vice Marshal Bill Hely. In this role, Headlam was involved with the Air Board, the service’s governing body composed of senior officers and led by the Chief of the Air Staff. Additionally, he was one of two RAAF representatives on a committee chaired by businessman William John Allison, which evaluated conditions for defense personnel; the committee's recommendations led to a significant rise in flight pay, among other benefits. Moreover, Headlam held other positions within the Department of Air, including Air Commodore Plans from October 1957 to January 1959, and Director General Plans and Policy from January to August 1959, the latter role placing him in charge of the RAAF's Directorate of Intelligence. He was recognized as a Commander of the Order of the British Empire (CBE) during the 1958 Queen's Birthday Honours, announced on June 3. In May 1960, he assumed the position of acting Deputy Chief of the Air Staff.

On January 30, 1961, Headlam joined the Operational Command (OPCOM) team, which had taken over the duties from Home Command to manage RAAF operational units. In April, he took over from Air Vice Marshal Val Hancock as the Air Officer Commanding (AOC) of OPCOM. He attained the rank of air vice marshal on May 29. On July 17, 1962, he was posted to RAAF Base Butterworth in Malaya, and just a week later, he began serving as the AOC for No. 224 Group RAF in Singapore. Air Vice Marshal Alister Murdoch succeeded him as AOC OPCOM. During his tenure as AOC for No. 224 Group, Headlam oversaw regional air defense and offensive air operations amid the Brunei Rebellion in December 1962, followed by the start of the Konfrontasi between Indonesia and Malaysia, which officially commenced the following month. After divorcing his first wife in 1956, he wed the widowed social worker Vernon Spence at the Sydney registry office on January 20, 1964. He passed command of No. 224 Group to Air Vice Marshal Christopher Foxley-Norris on November 30.

Upon returning to Australia, Headlam assumed the position of Deputy Chief of the Air Staff (DCAS) on 26 January 1965. He was honored with the title of Companion of the Order of the Bath (CB) on 22 June for his "distinguished service in the Borneo Territories." His tenure as DCAS coincided with the Air Force's most substantial rearmament effort since World War II, a process made more challenging by staffing shortages due to this expansion and Australia's increasing security responsibilities in Southeast Asia. Near the conclusion of his term, the first RAAF helicopters were sent to the Vietnam War; in March 1966, he traveled to Saigon with Lieutenant General Sir John Wilton, the Chief of the General Staff, to discuss deployment strategies. A year earlier, Wilton had proposed to Air Marshal Murdoch, the Chief of the Air Staff, the idea of dispatching two Iroquois helicopters to Vietnam for training, but Murdoch rejected the idea, leaving the RAAF helicopter squadron ill-equipped for its cooperative role with the army upon arrival. On 8 August 1966, Headlam succeeded Air Vice Marshal Douglas Candy as Air Officer Commanding Support Command in Melbourne, which had been formed in 1959 by merging the RAAF’s former Training and Maintenance Commands. He was later appointed to London on 1 January 1968 as Head of the Australian Joint Services Staff. Additionally, he held the position of Extra Gentleman Usher to the Queen from 17 November 1970 to 5 June 1971.

After returning to Australia in June 1971, Headlam took some time off for resettlement before retiring from the Air Force on August 3. He made his home in Melbourne, where he died at the age of 62 on December 23, 1976, after a prolonged battle with cancer. He is survived by his children and his second wife. A private funeral was conducted, and he was cremated at Springvale Crematorium.

M-82 is an important trunkline in the Lower Peninsula of Michigan, USA, linking Fremont and Howard City. The segment between Newaygo and Howard City traverses Fremont and follows the southern edge of the Manistee National Forest. This version of M-82 is the state's second; the first was established in the Upper Peninsula around 1919. The route in the Lower Peninsula has remained mostly stable since the 1920s, though there have been several extensions and reductions that have shifted the endpoint as far west as New Era or Hesperia. The present alignment was set in the late 1970s.

M @-@ 82 begins at an intersection with M @-@ 120 and B @-@ 96, situated to the west of Fremont. This point signifies the meeting of three county borders. M @-@ 120 acts as the north-south divider between Newaygo and Oceana counties, as well as between Newaygo and Muskegon counties. Meanwhile, B @-@ 96 marks the east-west boundary for Oceana and Muskegon counties, extending directly west of the junction. From this location, M @-@ 82 heads east along 48th Street, passing through agricultural regions until it reaches Fremont. Upon entering the town, it transforms into Main Street, traversing the downtown area before M @-@ 82 turns south onto Stewart Avenue while exiting the city. The highway then bends onto 72nd Street, continuing eastward through further farming landscapes. As M @-@ 82 nears Newaygo, the surroundings grow more wooded near the Muskegon River. The route continues along Fremont Street until it meets M @-@ 37. The two highways combine, crossing the river and entering downtown along State Street. Just south of downtown, M @-@ 82 veers east again, diverging from M @-@ 37, and follows 82nd Street along the southern edge of the Manistee National Forest. The eastern end of M @-@ 82 is located at exit 118 on US 131 / M @-@ 46, to the west of Howard City.

The Michigan Department of Transportation (MDOT) is responsible for maintaining its roadways and regularly monitors traffic patterns. This monitoring is done using a metric known as average annual daily traffic (AADT), which indicates the average number of vehicles that travel on a specific road segment each day over the course of a year. In 2009, MDOT noted that the highest traffic volume on M-82, located west of Fremont, reached 16,532 vehicles daily. In contrast, the lowest volume recorded was 4,018 vehicles to the east of Newaygo. Additionally, MDOT has not classified any section of this highway as part of the National Highway System, which includes roads vital to the nation's economy, defense, and transportation network.

The present M-82 was created in 1926, running from US 31 in Hart to the northern intersection of US 131 and M-46 in Howard City. This route traversed through Ferry, Hesperia, and Fremont, replacing the former M-41 alignment. In late 1936, M-46 was extended to connect Newaygo with Howard City, establishing a concurrency with M-82 to fill a gap in the M-46 route. By 1938, this shared segment was reclassified solely as M-46, which reverted M-82 to its northern junction with M-37 in Newaygo. In late 1947 or early 1948, the highway was realigned along a new route west of Ferry, altering its direction from northwest toward Hart to a westbound terminus in Shelby.

In 1963 and 1964, the western portion of the highway experienced two realignments, stretching from Hesperia to New Era while avoiding Ferry. A major change took place around 1969, leading to a reorganization of highway designations in Oceana County. M-20 replaced M-82 west of Hesperia, terminating at New Era instead of Muskegon. Concurrently, M-120 assumed control of the segment south of Hesperia, while M-82 was confined to the route linking Hesperia and Newaygo. In 1973, the highway's length was increased as the eastern terminus was moved back to Howard City. M-46 was rerouted to connect with the US 131 freeway from Howard City to Cedar Springs, taking over M-57 between Cedar Springs and Casnovia. This change allowed the stretch from Newaygo to Howard City to revert to the M-82 designation. The final adjustment occurred in 1978, when the overlap with M-120 was eliminated in favor of M-120. As a result, the M-82 designation was restricted to the junction west of Fremont, finalizing the current route of the highway.

Shikamaru Nara (Nara Shikamaru) is a character from the Naruto manga and anime series created by Masashi Kishimoto. Shikamaru has consistently ranked highly in the Weekly Shōnen Jump popularity polls, often placing in the top ten and notably reaching fourth place at least once. In the latest poll, held in 2011, he secured ninth place, positioned between Sasori and Hinata. A variety of merchandise featuring Shikamaru has been released, including action figures, keychains, and patches that highlight his appearances from both Part I and Part II. Furthermore, NTT customers have identified him as the sixteenth most popular black-haired male anime character. Hiroshi Matsuyama, the CEO of CyberConnect2, has stated that Shikamaru is one of his favorite characters from Naruto.

Numerous articles exploring manga, anime, video games, and related media have analyzed Shikamaru's character. IGN recognized Shikamaru as one of their top characters in the series, labeling him as "the poster child for any card-carrying member of Generation X" due to his prevailing indifference and hesitance to realize his full potential. In their review of episode 110, IGN praised Shikamaru for breaking free from his lazy tendencies and stepping up as a leader in the mission to rescue Sasuke Uchiha, agreeing that his advancement to Chunin was well-deserved. Anime News Network also noted this change, describing Shikamaru's evolution into "an unlikely hero" as a highlight of the arc. In a subsequent review of episode 135, where the attempt to rescue Sasuke was unsuccessful and Shikamaru's team faced severe injuries, IGN emphasized the "great moment" when Shikamaru cried upon hearing that his friends would heal, underscoring that he would grow into a more capable leader for them. Justin Rich from Mania Entertainment lauded Shikamaru's "sheer intellect," calling him "one of the most fascinating characters in the series" and "one of the few genuinely brilliant fighters in shōnen anime." Dani Moure, another reviewer from the same publication, highlighted Shikamaru's clash with Temari during the Chunin Exams as "one of the better battles featuring supporting characters."

Meridian ranks as the sixth largest city in Mississippi, USA, and acts as the county seat for Lauderdale County. It is the principal city within the Meridian, Mississippi Micropolitan Statistical Area. The city is strategically situated along major highways, lying 93 miles (150 kilometers) to the east of Jackson, Mississippi; 154 miles (248 kilometers) to the west of Birmingham, Alabama; 202 miles (325 kilometers) to the northeast of New Orleans, Louisiana; and 231 miles (372 kilometers) to the southeast of Memphis, Tennessee.

Established in 1860 at the intersection of the Mobile and Ohio Railroad and the Southern Railway of Mississippi, Meridian’s economy grew in connection with the railroads and the products they transported, positioning it as an important trading center. In February 1864, amid the American Civil War, General William Tecumseh Sherman ignited a large section of the city during the Battle of Meridian.

Following the war, the city experienced a reconstruction phase and entered a period referred to as a "Golden Age," during which it became the largest city in Mississippi from 1890 to 1930 and transformed into a significant manufacturing center in the South, with 44 trains operating daily. Union Station, inaugurated in 1906, currently functions as a multi-modal transportation hub, connecting to the Meridian Transit System, Greyhound Buses, and Trailways, serving approximately 242,360 passengers each year. Despite encountering economic challenges due to a decline in the railroad sector, the city effectively diversified its economy, with the healthcare, military, and manufacturing sectors providing the majority of employment by 2010. As per the 2008 census, the estimated population within the city limits stands at 38,232, while the broader population within a 45-mile (72 km) radius reaches 232,900, and 526,500 within a 65-mile (105 km) radius, with 104,600 and 234,200 individuals respectively contributing to the labor force and bolstering the city's economy.

The area is supported by two military bases: Naval Air Station Meridian and Key Field, which together provide over 4,000 job positions. NAS Meridian is home to the Regional Counter-Drug Training Academy and holds the distinction of being the first office of the Department of Homeland Security established in the state. Key Field is named after brothers Fred and Al Key, who achieved a world endurance flight record in 1935. Presently, the field accommodates the 186th Air Refueling Wing of the Air National Guard and serves as a facility for the 185th Aviation Brigade of the Army National Guard. Furthermore, Rush Foundation Hospital is the largest non-military employer in the region, offering jobs to 2,610 people.

Among the city's rich variety of cultural organizations and historical buildings are the Riley Center, the Meridian Museum of Art, Meridian Little Theatre, and the Meridian Symphony Orchestra. Meridian previously had two Carnegie libraries that served both the white and African American populations. The Carnegie Branch Library, which has since been torn down, was one of several Carnegie libraries created for African Americans in the Southern United States during the era of segregation.

The city has been selected as the future location for the Mississippi Arts and Entertainment Center. Jimmie Rodgers, often referred to as the "Father of Country Music," was born in Meridian. Within Highland Park, there is a museum dedicated to his life and career, featuring memorabilia and artifacts from the steam engine era. The park is also home to the Highland Park Dentzel Carousel, recognized as a National Historic Landmark and the last two-row stationary Dentzel menagerie still in existence worldwide. Other distinguished individuals from the region include Susan Akin, Miss America 1986; James Chaney, an activist who was killed during the Mississippi civil rights movement in 1964; and Hartley Peavey, the founder of Peavey Electronics, headquartered in Meridian. The federal courthouse was the venue for the trial from 1966 to 1967 for those accused in the murders of Chaney and two other activists; this trial was notable as it was the first time a white jury convicted a white official for a murder linked to civil rights.

The area currently referred to as Meridian was initially inhabited by the Choctaw Native Americans and came under U.S. control through the Treaty of Dancing Rabbit Creek in 1830, during the period of Indian Removal. After the treaty was ratified, European American settlers started to move into the region.

After receiving a federal land grant of around 2,000 acres (810 hectares), Richard McLemore, the first settler of Meridian, began offering free land to entice newcomers and foster growth in the region. In 1853, Lewis A. Ragsdale, a lawyer from Alabama, bought most of McLemore's land. The leftover 80 acres (0.32 km²) were purchased by John T. Ball, a merchant from Kemper County. Acknowledged as the founders of the city, Ragsdale and Ball initiated the process of subdividing their respective parcels into lots for future development.

A major conflict arose over the settlement's name. Ball and the local industrial residents preferred "Meridian," equating it with "junction." Conversely, the farming community advocated for "<unk>" (meaning "mad river" in a Native American language), named after a nearby stream. Ragsdale proposed the name "Ragsdale City." In an effort to promote this name, Ball built a station house on the Mobile and Ohio Railroad, where a sign alternated daily between "Meridian" and "<unk>." Ultimately, the rapid growth of the railroads attracted a large number of railroad workers, who surpassed the other residents in number and solidified "Meridian" as the station's official designation. The town was formally incorporated as Meridian on February 10, 1860.

At the beginning of the American Civil War in 1861, Meridian was just a small settlement. Its strategic position at a railroad junction led the Confederacy to create several military posts to enhance their efforts during the war. In 1864, during the Battle of Meridian, General William Tecumseh Sherman marched his forces into the town, destroying the railroads in all directions, along with an arsenal and large storage facilities; a significant portion of the town's infrastructure was set on fire. Sherman reportedly stated afterward, "Meridian, with its depots, storehouses, arsenal, hospitals, offices, hotels, and cantonments no longer exists." However, the city's railroad lines were quickly repaired, and activities resumed within just 26 working days after the battle. Throughout the Reconstruction period, racial tensions remained elevated, highlighted by the riot in 1871 that broke out following a fire that damaged multiple businesses.

After the Civil War, the town saw substantial development and entered a prosperous phase known as its "Golden Age" from 1880 to 1910. The arrival of railroads improved transportation and drew in various industries, resulting in a population boom. With the rise in residents, commercial activities flourished in the downtown area. From 1890 to 1930, Meridian became the largest city in Mississippi and a significant manufacturing center in the South. Many of the city’s notable historical buildings were erected during this time and shortly after, including the Grand Opera House, which opened its doors in 1890, the Wechsler School established in 1894, two Carnegie libraries that were built in 1913, and the <unk> Building, finished in 1929, which became the tallest skyscraper in Meridian.

The city underwent significant growth, propelled by a commission government that set out to create 90 new industrial sites in 1913, coupled with a burgeoning automobile industry in the 1920s. Despite the 1929 stock market crash and the ensuing Great Depression, the city succeeded in attracting new enterprises. During the challenging times of the Depression, the S. H. Kress & Co. building was inaugurated in downtown Meridian, intended to "bring luxury to the average person," alongside the Temple Theater, which served as a cinema. Moreover, the federal courthouse was built in 1933 as part of a WPA project.

After a brief economic downturn at the end of the Depression, the country entered World War II, which renewed the importance of railroads. The railways played a vital role in moving gasoline and scrap metal needed for military vehicle production, contributing to the revival of Meridian as the region's railway center. This economic upturn continued until the 1950s, when cars and the Interstate Highway System began to take precedence over passenger trains. The decline in the railroad industry led to significant job losses, causing a population decrease as workers relocated elsewhere.

In the 1960s, amid the American Civil Rights Movement, Meridian served as a base for the Council of Federated Organizations (CFO) and various other activist groups. Local activists such as James Chaney, along with Michael <unk>, his spouse Rita, and Andrew Goodman—who were volunteers from the North—sought to create a community center that provided classes designed to empower African Americans in the area to reclaim their voting rights. This activism sparked outrage among local white residents, frequently resulting in violence as racial tensions intensified. In June 1964, Chaney, <unk>, and Goodman went to Neshoba County, Mississippi, to meet with members of a black church that had suffered from a bombing and arson attack. That evening, while heading back to Meridian, the three vanished. Following a thorough investigation by the FBI, their bodies were found two months later, buried in an earthen dam.

At a federal courthouse in Meridian, seven members of the Ku Klux Klan, including a deputy sheriff, were found guilty of "depriving the victims of their civil rights," while three others were acquitted during the trial related to the murders of civil rights activists in Mississippi. This case represented the first time a white jury convicted "a white official in a civil rights homicide." In 2005, the investigation was revisited by the state, resulting in charges being filed for the first time. Edgar Ray Killen was convicted of manslaughter and sentenced to 60 years in prison. To honor Chaney, a part of 49th Avenue in Meridian was renamed after him, and an annual memorial service was established.

Starting in the 1960s, the expansion of highways made commuting easier, prompting individuals to move from the city center to newly built residential areas in the northern parts. As strip malls began to invade downtown, the city responded in the 1970s and 1980s by designating several zones as historic districts to preserve the city's architectural heritage. In 1979, the Meridian Historic Districts and Landmarks Commission was formed, and in 1985, the Meridian Main Street program was initiated.

Meridian Main Street launched various initiatives to revitalize the downtown district, which included the opening of a new Amtrak Station in 1997, inspired by the old train station that once served the city during its peak before it was torn down. Other efforts involved the restoration of the Rosenbaum Building in 2001 and Weidmann's Restaurant in 2002, as well as promoting cohesive urban design. Partnering with The Riley Foundation, Meridian Main Street was instrumental in the renovation of the historic Grand Opera House in 2006, transforming it into the "Mississippi State University Riley Center for Education and the Performing Arts."

After the ownership of Meridian Main Street was transferred to the Alliance for Downtown Meridian in late 2007, both organizations, along with the Meridian Downtown Association, took the initiative to revitalize the downtown district. The Alliance serves as a central entity, offering support staff and resources to the other two groups and acting as a communication bridge among them. Although there were plans to renovate the <unk> Building, newly elected Mayor Cheri Barry put those plans on hold in early 2010. Currently, the Alliance is dedicated to encouraging further development and restoration in downtown, with a focus on supporting businesses such as specialty shops, restaurants, and bars that enhance a vibrant atmosphere both during the day and at night. At the same time, the Meridian Downtown Association is working to increase foot traffic in the area by organizing special events, while the Meridian Main Street program aims to assist the local businesses in the neighborhood.

Meridian's role as a railway hub has stimulated the development of numerous hotels aimed at travelers. Even before the onset of Meridian's "Golden Age," several notable hotels, including the Great Southern and the Grand Avenue, were established prior to the 20th century. The growth of railroads and the opening of the original Union Station in 1906 spurred the creation of more hotels to accommodate both passengers and workers. The Elmira Hotel was constructed in 1905, followed by the Terminal Hotel in 1910. Hotel Meridian was launched in 1907, and the Union Hotel was established in 1908. In 1979, the Union Hotel was listed on the National Register of Historic Places, while both Hotel Meridian and the Grand Avenue Hotel were acknowledged as important sites within the Meridian Urban Center Historic District.

With the city's growth, its hotels reflected the ambitions of a thriving economy, notably represented by the Lamar Hotel, an eleven-story structure completed in 1927. This hotel was included in the National Register of Historic Places in 1979 and subsequently converted into a county annex building. In 1988, it was designated as a Mississippi Landmark.

Built in 1931, the E.F. Young Hotel became an important establishment in the African American business district that developed to the west of downtown. During the period of segregation, it stood out as one of the limited places in the city that provided lodging for African American visitors.

In the 1960s and 1970s, the growth of suburban areas resulted in many hotels moving away from city centers. The revitalization of the Riley Center in 2006 increased the need for a new hotel in the downtown area. A plan was proposed to convert the <unk> Building for this purpose, but the renovation faced setbacks due to changes in city leadership. In 2013, the <unk> Preservation Society was formed to raise public awareness and support for the building's restoration, offering first-floor tours and organizing anniversary events.

Meridian is home to nine historic districts listed on the National Register of Historic Places. The Meridian Downtown Historic District merges two earlier districts: the Meridian Urban Center Historic District and the Union Station Historic District. These areas highlight a range of architectural styles, mainly from the late 19th and early 20th centuries, including Queen Anne, Colonial Revival, Italianate, Art Deco, Late Victorian, and Bungalow styles. Since 1985, Meridian has operated under a mayor-council or "strong mayor" governance model. The mayor is elected by the entire electorate every four years. In addition, five city council members are elected every four years, each representing one of the five wards, which are considered single-member districts. Serving as the city's chief executive officer, the mayor manages and guides the daily functions of the city government. In contrast, the city council acts as the legislative body, responsible for developing policies and approving the city's yearly budget.

City Hall, listed on the National Register of Historic Places, is located at 601 23rd Avenue. Percy Bland currently serves as the mayor. The city council includes Dr. George M. Thomas from Ward 1, Kenneth Dustin Markham from Ward 2, Barbara Henson from Ward 3, Kim Houston from Ward 4, and Randy Hammon from Ward 5. Pam McInnis acts as the council clerk. In total, the city has 570 employees.

After Hurricane Katrina struck in 2005, the city established a Department of Homeland Security (DHS), making it the only local DHS in the state. This department oversees a jurisdiction that spans nine counties. With $2.5 million in funding obtained from the Mississippi Emergency Management Agency and various other organizations, the department launched training programs for law enforcement officers from neighboring Southern states in passenger rail rescue techniques, as well as offering civilian courses in basic handgun proficiency, first aid for Boy Scouts, hunting, and firearm education. The DHS is crucial during emergencies, as demonstrated during Hurricane Ivan in September 2005, when it helped set up and manage shelters for 700 evacuees. At present, the city heads one of the task forces within the Mississippi DHS, which consists of three teams, each covering nine counties.

Since 2009, led by Police Chief Lee <unk>, the Meridian Police Department has consisted of 115 full-time officers, along with part-time and reserve staff. In that same year, the Criminal Investigations Division managed 4,000 cases, of which 2,000 were categorized as felonies. Crime statistics for 2009 showed a minor rise compared to the previous year. Meridian is recognized as "the safest city in Mississippi with a population over 30,000." The East Mississippi Correctional Facility, situated in unincorporated Lauderdale County near Meridian, is operated by the GEO Group on behalf of the Mississippi Department of Corrections. Additionally, the Meridian Fire Department, directed by Chief Anthony Clayton, responded to more than 1,600 calls in 2009, which included 123 structural fires and 609 emergency service incidents.

In the domain of state politics, the Senate district map of Mississippi divides the city into three separate zones. The northernmost area belongs to the 31st State Senate District, with Terry Clark Burton (R) as its representative. A corridor that stretches from the southwest to the northeast corner of the city falls under the 32nd State Senate District, represented by Sampson Jackson, II (D). The western and southeastern sections of the city are part of the 33rd State Senate District, which is represented by <unk> Carmichael (R). Regarding the Mississippi House of Representatives, the city is split into four districts. The southern and eastern areas are contained within House District 81, represented by Steven A. Horne (R). The central portion of the city comprises all of House District 82, represented by Wilbert L. Jones (D). Encircling House District 82 is House District 83, whose representative is Greg Snowden (R). Lastly, the western segment of the city, along with a small northern area, falls under House District 84, represented by Tad Campbell (R).

At the national level, the city is part of Mississippi's 3rd congressional district, currently represented by Gregg Harper (R), who has been in office since 2009. Meridian is situated in Lauderdale County, which has reliably supported the Republican candidate in all U.S. presidential elections since 1972. Prior to this shift towards the Republican Party, the area's white voters mainly favored Democratic candidates, as the region was largely dominated by one political party for several decades after the late 19th century.

The city's development has reflected the impact of various social and economic factors. From its founding until 1970, the population steadily grew with each census, although the growth rates varied greatly, peaking at 165% and plummeting to a mere 0.2%. The 1970 census showed a population decline, but by 1980, there was a slight increase, which was followed by a steady decrease until the early 21st century when growth resumed. From 1980 to 2000, the population fell by more than 14%. The 2000 census recorded a population of 39,968, translating to a density of 885.9 residents per square mile (342.0/km²). By 2008, the city had become the sixth largest in the state, and an increase in population was observed in 2010.

Meridian acts as the primary city of the Meridian area, which, as of 2009, encompassed three counties: Clarke, Kemper, and Lauderdale, with a total population of 106,139. The population within a 45-mile (72 km) radius is 232,900, and it increases to 526,500 when considering a 65-mile (105 km) radius.

While the city's total population has experienced fluctuations, there has been a steady rise in both the quantity and percentage of non-white residents. The sole decline in this demographic took place between 1960 and 1970, which coincided with a notable decrease in the city’s overall population. The 2010 Census revealed that the racial makeup of the city included 61.55% African American, 35.71% White, 0.09% Asian, 0.2% Native American, less than 0.02% Pacific Islander, 0.59% from other races, and 0.89% identifying as two or more races. Additionally, those who identified as Hispanic or Latino of any race made up 1.75% of the population.

According to the 2000 Census, the city had a total of 17,890 housing units, with 15,966 of these being occupied; out of the occupied units, 10,033 were family residences. Among the occupied homes, 31.1% housed children under 18 years old, 36.2% consisted of married couples, 23.3% were led by female householders without a spouse, and 37.2% were categorized as non-family households. Individuals represented 33.2% of all households, and 14.0% included at least one resident aged 65 or older living alone. The average household size was 2.39, while family households averaged 3.06 members. Since 1970, there has been a steady decline in average household size from 3.04. Furthermore, the median age in Meridian increased from 30.4 in 1970 to 34.6 in 2000.

The median household income in the city was $25,085, whereas the median income for families was $31,062. Males had a median income of $29,404, in contrast to females, who earned a median of $19,702. The per capita income for the city was recorded at $15,255. Around 24.6% of families and 28.6% of the total population were living below the poverty threshold, which encompassed 40.8% of individuals under 18 years old and 22.0% of those aged 65 and above.

The population of Meridian and its nearby regions demonstrates a high level of religious engagement, as 65.2% of Lauderdale County residents indicated they belong to a religious organization, which is above the national average of 50.2%. In 2000, of those who identified with a faith, 30,068 individuals (59.0%) were associated with the Southern Baptist Convention, 9,469 (18.6%) were part of the United Methodist Church, and 1,872 (3.7%) were connected to the Catholic Church.

Jewish immigrants from Germany and Eastern Europe significantly contributed to the city's economic development by founding numerous businesses and services. Congregation Beth Israel was formed in 1868, just prior to the city's "Golden Age." By 1927, Meridian had the largest Jewish population in the state, with 575 members. Today, however, fewer than 40 Jews live in Meridian, most of whom are elderly.

Meridian is located in the North Central Hills area of Mississippi, specifically within Lauderdale County. As reported by the United States Census Bureau, the city covers an area of 45.9 square miles (119 km²), which includes 45.1 square miles (117 km²) of land and 0.8 square miles (2.1 km²) of water. In terms of its location relative to major highways, Meridian is positioned 93 miles (150 km) east of Jackson, Mississippi; 154 miles (248 km) west of Birmingham, Alabama; 202 miles (325 km) northeast of New Orleans, Louisiana; 231 miles (372 km) southeast of Memphis, Tennessee; and 297 miles (478 km) west of Atlanta, Georgia. The surrounding landscape features cotton and corn fields along with oak and pine forests, creating a terrain of clay hills and low-lying areas near the headwaters of an unnamed river.

The urban center of the city has transformed its natural terrain by flattening it, but the nearby areas still showcase gently rolling hills. Numerous small creeks, as well as lakes and wooded spaces, are dispersed across the city, particularly in the northern and southern parts. <unk> Creek flows through the southern area and branches into Gallagher's Creek, which cuts through the heart of the city. To the far west, Loper's Creek can be found, while various smaller creeks like Shearer’s Branch, Magnolia Creek, and Robbins Creek are found throughout the city.

Meridian is located in a humid subtropical climate region. During the summer months (June to August), the typical high temperature is around 90 °F (32 °C), with an average low of about 70 °F (21 °C). In contrast, the winter season (December to February) sees the average high temperature decrease to approximately 60 °F (16 °C), and the average low falls to around 35 °F (2 °C). July is usually the hottest month, with an average high of 92.9 °F (33.8 °C), while January is recognized as the coldest month, having an average low of 34.7 °F (1.5 °C).

The city experiences an annual average rainfall of 58.65 inches (1,490 mm). Precipitation is fairly steady throughout the year, with March being the month that receives the most rain, averaging 6.93 inches (176 mm). A large portion of this rainfall is attributed to thunderstorms, which are common during the summer months but can occur at any time of the year. Intense thunderstorms can cause damaging winds and large hail, alongside the usual dangers related to lightning and heavy rainfall. These severe weather occurrences are most commonly observed in the spring, with another peak in the fall. Moreover, these storms have the capability to spawn tornadoes.

In its formative years, the economy was largely dependent on the region's railroads. By the early 20th century, the city had emerged as the largest in Mississippi, boasting five major rail lines and 44 trains operating daily. The local economy was intricately linked not just to the railroads but also to the products they transported, such as timber and cotton. From around 1890 to 1930, these railroad-dependent industries played a crucial role in establishing the city as a key economic player in the state and nearby regions. Although the city faced economic challenges due to the downturn of the railroad sector in the 1950s, it adeptly shifted from a railroad-centric economy to a more varied one, with healthcare, military, and manufacturing now accounting for most of the employment opportunities.

Meridian, together with Lauderdale County and the city of Marion, gains from the East Mississippi Business Development Corporation, which was founded by local entrepreneurs in 1996. By April 2010, the city had a civilian labor force numbering 15,420, with a population of 232,900 in a 45-mile (72 km) radius and 526,500 in a 65-mile (105 km) radius, resulting in labor force estimates of 104,600 and 234,200, respectively. As a result, the city serves as a hub for employment, retail, healthcare, and cultural pursuits. Eighty percent of Lauderdale County's workforce resides within the county, while 90% live within 45 miles.

As of April 2010, the healthcare industry in Lauderdale County provided jobs for a total of 6,260 people. The primary healthcare provider in the region is Rush Hospital, employing 2,610 staff members, followed by East Mississippi State Hospital with 1,500 employees and Anderson Hospital, which has a workforce of 1,475. Meridian hosts three hospitals along with various other healthcare facilities. Jeff Anderson Regional Medical Center offers services such as cardiovascular surgery, a Level II neonatal intensive care unit, and a health and fitness center. Furthermore, Rush Foundation Hospital, in partnership with Rush Health Systems, oversees the Specialty Hospital of Meridian, which focuses on long-term care for patients requiring extended recovery in a hospital setting. Riley Hospital includes two centers dedicated to stroke treatment and rehabilitation services. Other healthcare establishments in Meridian comprise the Alliance Health Center and East Mississippi State Hospital, a community resource that has been operational since 1882.

The retail sector plays a crucial role in county employment, with 5,280 people employed in this field as of April 2010. Each year, roughly $2 billion is spent on retail in the city. The Bonita Lakes Mall covers an area of 633,685 square feet (58,871 m²) and offers more than one hundred shopping choices, including department stores, specialty shops, restaurants, and United Artists Theatres. The first phase of the Meridian Crossroads shopping center, which spans 375,000 square feet (34,800 m²) in the Bonita Lakes region, was completed in November 2007, greatly improving the local retail environment. Furthermore, the shopping area on North Hills Street has been expanding, with new retail and office developments opening in March 2007 near the Walmart Supercenter on Highway 19.

The area benefits from two military bases, Naval Air Station Meridian and Key Field, which together create over 4,000 jobs for local residents. NAS Meridian is tasked with training naval carrier pilots and various enlisted personnel, and it is home to the Regional Counter-Drug Training Academy (RCDTA), which provides drug enforcement training to law enforcement agencies in multiple southeastern states. The city proudly features the state's first local Department of Homeland Security and serves as a key leader for a nine-county regional response team, as well as a twenty-nine county regional response task force. Key Field is historically significant due to the record-setting endurance flight by brothers Fred and Al Key in 1935. Presently, Key Field hosts the 186th Air Refueling Wing of the Air National Guard and serves as a support facility for the 185th Aviation Brigade of the Army National Guard. Additionally, the site includes an exhibit focused on aviation history and is home to Meridian's Aviation Museum.

In April 2010, Lauderdale County's manufacturing sector employed 2,850 people. The Peavey Electronics Corporation, established in 1965, has been manufacturing guitars, amplifiers, and audio equipment in the city. Other notable businesses in the area include Avery Dennison, Structural Steel Services, Sara Lee, Tower Automotive, and <unk> Corporation. The city is home to four industrial parks as well.

Situated in the center of downtown, the MSU Riley Center generates revenue through tourism while fostering arts and entertainment. Annually, the Riley Center attracts more than 60,000 visitors to downtown Meridian for a range of conferences, meetings, and performances. At the same time, Loeb's Department Store on Front Street has been a prominent clothing retailer in Mississippi, remaining under family ownership for four generations. Founded by Alex Loeb in 1887, the store has consistently provided high-quality clothing for men and women.

Meridian boasts a rich artistic heritage that spans more than a century, featuring numerous cultural organizations and events. Established in February 1933, the Meridian Art League stands as one of the city's pioneering art institutions. Initially, art exhibitions were held at the Lamar Hotel in downtown Meridian, but in 1949, the organization was renamed the Meridian Art Association and began showcasing exhibitions in various locations throughout the city. After the Carnegie Library at 25th Ave and 7th St closed, the Art Association converted the space into the Meridian Museum of Art, providing a dedicated venue for its exhibits. The museum opened in 1970 and has since hosted a rotating series of exhibitions, along with a broad array of educational programs for both adults and students. Each year, the museum features over thirty exhibitions that highlight a wide variety of artwork, including traditional decorative arts, ethnographic and tribal items, photography, crafts, and more. Its collection includes portraits from the 18th and 19th centuries, 20th-century photography, and various sculptures.

The Meridian Council for the Arts (MCA) was founded in 1978 as the designated arts agency for Meridian and Lauderdale County. MCA oversees the Community Art Grants program, organizes the annual <unk> Festival, provides various workshops, and coordinates a wide range of special events each year. The council works in partnership with several arts organizations within the city and county, including the Meridian Museum of Art, the Meridian Little Theatre, and the Meridian Symphony Orchestra. The Meridian Little Theatre, recognized as one of the oldest subscription community theaters in the Southern United States, was built in 1932 and draws over 22,000 visitors each season, making it the most popular community theater in Mississippi. Founded in 1961, the Meridian Symphony Orchestra (<unk>) held its first concert in 1962 and commenced its inaugural full season in 1963. In 1965, the <unk> featured its first international soloist, Elena <unk>, who performed with the orchestra. Furthermore, the Orchestra has assisted the Meridian Public School District in developing its own orchestra and strings programs and contributed to the formation of the Meridian Symphony Chorus. Dr. Claire Fox Hillard, who has been conducting since 1991, currently directs the orchestra, which is scheduled to celebrate its 50th anniversary in February 2011 with a performance by Itzhak Perlman.

The Grand Opera House, founded in 1889 by half-brothers Israel Marks and Levi Rothenberg, boasts a storied legacy of presenting numerous celebrated artists and performances, beginning with a German troupe's staging of Johann Strauss II’s "The Gypsy Baron." However, the opera house shut its doors in the late 1920s due to the Great Depression and stood in disrepair for nearly seventy years. In 2000, a significant restoration project commenced, backed by a $10 million grant from the locally established Riley Foundation in 1998, along with an additional $15 million sourced from a combination of city, county, and federal funding. The renovation was completed in September 2006, and the venue was renamed the "Mississippi State University Riley Center for Education and Performing Arts." The Riley Center includes a 950-seat auditorium for live performances, a 200-seat studio theater, and 30,000 square feet (2,787 m²) of meeting space, attracting over 60,000 visitors each year to downtown Meridian for conferences, meetings, and shows.

Meridian is justly renowned as an architectural treasure, acknowledged as one of the best-preserved early 20th-century cities in the U.S. Architecture students from various universities in the U.S. and Canada often travel to Meridian in groups for their studies, drawn by its many buildings designed by notable architects. Among its landmarks is the sole residence in the Southern United States created by the distinguished Canadian architect Louis S. The public education system in Meridian was first established under the Mississippi Constitution of 1870. "Angel of Death" is the opening song on Slayer's 1986 album, Reign in Blood, by the American thrash metal group. As a result, the band has faced various accusations of Nazi sympathies and racism throughout their career.

Despite discussions surrounding the song and its impact on delaying the release of Reign in Blood, "Angel of Death" appears in all of Slayer's live albums and DVDs, and has been showcased in several films. The track has received acclaim from critics, with Steve Huey of AllMusic describing it as a "classic."

Jeff Hanneman, the guitarist for Slayer, wrote "Angel of Death" after exploring literature on Nazi doctor Josef Mengele while the band was touring. He reminisced, "I remember stopping at a place where I bought two books about Mengele. I thought, 'This has to contain some dark material.' So, when it came time to work on the album, those ideas were still vivid in my mind — that’s what inspired the lyrics of 'Angel of Death.'"

The lyrics detail the surgical experiments carried out by Mengele on prisoners at Auschwitz during World War II. His research focused on particular demographics, especially dwarfs and twins, and involved both physical and psychological evaluations. The song "Angel of Death" alludes to numerous procedures he executed, such as surgeries conducted without anesthesia, blood transfusions between twins, confinement for endurance testing, gassing, lethal pathogen injections, sex reassignment operations, and the extraction of organs and limbs, among other practices.

"Uniting their efforts, but it’s only a question of time before you end up at odds," is a line from the second-to-last verse that refers to allegations that Mengele conducted experiments on twins, one of whom had a physical deformity. Reports suggest that "the hunchback was stitched to the other child, back to back, with their wrists also linked." This assertion was first brought to light by Auschwitz survivor Vera Alexander during the 1961 trial of SS officer Adolf Eichmann, known as the "architect of the Holocaust." It was claimed that Mengele "connected their veins" and turned them into Siamese twins. This allegation garnered more attention after Vera Alexander featured in the 1985 documentary The Search for Mengele, which has been cited by many authors, including Gerald Posner, a recognized authority on Mengele.

The lyrics of "Angel of Death" significantly contributed to the delay in the release of Slayer's 1986 album, Reign in Blood. Despite having an agreement with Def Jam Records, their distributor, Columbia Records, refused to release the album due to worries about its lyrical content and cover art, which they deemed "excessively graphic." In the end, Reign in Blood was released by Geffen Records on October 7, 1986. However, due to the controversy that arose, the album was not included in Geffen Records' official release lineup.
